utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we have the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to inform us? Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this involves the next witness proposed by the Prosecution, Mr. Manning. And we thought it would be untimely if we waited any longer, but we wanted to make an offer to the Prosecution that Dean Manning would be accepted as a witness under 92 bis (D) for the transcript to be admitted and under 94 bis (C); The opposing party accepts the statement of the witness. The statement may be admitted into evidence without calling the witness to testify. We have no objections to his report or his transcript being admitted into evidence and for the sake of expediency in the trial, I believe we have an agreement also with the counsel for Blagojevic. We think it would just be best to have his transcripts admitted through 94 bis (C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I hear Mr. Karnavas about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. In principle, we would not have any objections, however it has been brought to my attention that there is one particular issue that perhaps needs clarification through Dean Manning. And so while I did make representations to Ms. Sinatra yesterday that I did not think that would be a problem, that I would probably join her in this motion, in retrospect - and I didn't get a chance to discuss this with her - there is one minor issue. I don't -- having said that, I certainly don't think that his testimony is necessary for two full days, unless -- I know the Prosecution wants to -- well, I don't know what they want to do. Far be it for me to make recommendations to Mr. McCloskey, but I suspect he wants to get a lot of documents in and what have you. It appears that this is a witness that could be handled in less than a day or one day, perhaps. So I don't know if that is of any assistance. I would like to hear what the Prosecutor has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I am very encouraged by your submissions, Mr. Karnavas. And of course we should not ask anything about your case at this stage, but could you give us some indication how minor that issue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How minor that issue is? Well, it's an issue that would require confrontation of the witness. In all due -- it's not my position, it's not my approach to cross-examine every witness or to try to impeach every witness. I have a particular theory in mind of the points that I need to make. There are some points that I need to obviously question the gentleman on. On the majority of his testimony, I have no objection to it coming in. If the point was not relevant to the case, I certainly would not be standing here, especially as I indicated yesterday after discussing the matter with Ms. Sinatra, I did make representations to her that I would in all likelihood join her because obviously I don't -- I want to make sure I don't cause her any embarrassment on the record. But as I said, upon reflection, it appears that there's a point that I need to question the gentleman. Having said that, I think a lot of the testimony that the gentleman has to offer can be offered very quickly through the Prosecution, unless they wish to go document after document after document. It's a dog and pony show, that's what we call back home. They're entitled to do that. I'm not suggesting that that's his intention. So we could expedite Mr. Manning's testimony, but I think he probably will be needed for us. I don't know if that assists Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and in light of the representation by counsel for Blagojevic, either Dean Manning will testify or he won't testify. If he testifies we'll be forced to go through our full cross-examination also. But that's a decision that, I guess, the Trial Chamber will have to make. We're making an offer to allow his evidence to be presented through 94 bis (C). We agreed to that. If there are minor issues, then once the direct examination begins, they may become major issues and we were trying to forestall that. As the report exists at this time, we have no problems with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, could I hear from you about your view on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First, I haven't heard of any of this, Your Honour. I generally like the idea of discussing 92 bis. I would prefer to have time to discuss it prior to the moment of trial. But Ms. Issa will be putting on Mr. Manning and anticipates hopefully less than a day of direct. I think we put two days just because it was our estimate on what the Defence might want to do. And of course with this difficult period of trying to judge how far Mr. Butler would go, Mr. Manning seemed to fit well into that slot. As you know, much of what Mr. Manning will talk about is a summary on and a synthesis of what many experts have already testified about and have been accepted in the evidence as 92 bis. And in part Mr. Ruez's testimony was designed to fit in with Mr. Manning's testimony. So Mr. Manning's synthesis is an important part of our actual courtroom presentation, in that so much of this important evidence has come in through 92 bis. And so with less than a day of Prosecution material and we won't be bringing in any dogs or ponies, I think this is important evidence and the Prosecution would intend to put this evidence in in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So, Mr. McCloskey, you mean that you would like to have this witness as a live witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I forgot to mention that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Since we're talking about this issue, we recently got notice that they would like to have Mr. Deronjic come in through 92 bis and I would like to make sure and put everybody on notice that we vehemently oppose that. Because he's vital to our case, it's an integral part of the Prosecution's case. And of course, I think given that the Prosecution has indicated that they need someone like Dean Manning who is more or less a summary witness to come forward, to put on that sort of evidence, I think it would be reasonable that we would be allotted to have Mr. Deronjic who is a guest of the Detention Unit here. There is not any cost other than a trip to the Tribunal to come here and testify. So I just want to put everybody on notice on that, because we just received notice that they intend to try to move his testimony in in that manner. And of course it would be a violation of Mr. Blagojevic's right to confrontation. So I just thought I'd mention it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we agree that Mr. Deronjic's testimony should not come in. He is testifying, I believe, in the Krstic appeal hearing and they're trying to get that in through 92 bis, which is inappropriate. But going back to the issue of Mr. Manning, we still believe that the probative value of his testimony is outweighed by the prejudice, because all that the Prosecution wants to do is show the bodies and the forensics with this witness and to -- which it possibly inflames the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber has seen these videos. They understand it; they have 92 bis witness statements talking about the forensics involved. We believe that it is totally unnecessarily if we all accept the reports of this witness. If there's really nothing further, it's cumulative that this witness can offer at this point. So we one more time urge that Dean Manning's reports and transcripts from the Krstic trial under 92 bis (D) and 94 bis (C) be admitted without live testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, just regarding Mr. Deronjic, we just communicated that that possibility so we could begin discussions with the Defence about that. He is scheduled to testify. It's unclear exactly in my mind what the Appeals Chamber has and how complete his testimony will be, but what we're hoping is that it may form at least some complete part of this case and that we can offer that testimony into the record for 92 bis, perhaps put him on direct for a little bit, if necessary, and then open him up for cross. This was never meant to be a situation where Mr. Deronjic would be purely a paper, 92 bis, witness. So we understand the Defence's concern there, as is our concern. So that shouldn't be a problem. And that's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after the consultations with my colleagues, we decided that as for the witness of Mr. Manning, we are going to hear him live in this courtroom. But these proceedings should be very short and with the proper cross-examinations by the Defence of both parties. As for Mr. Deronjic's testimony, we believe that he could be a 92 bis witness with cross-examination, which means that the Prosecution should spend very little time in their direct. The main purpose of that direct examination is to draw our attention to certain particular important elements in his testimony, then we'll leave it to the Defence for the cross-examination. It is so decided. Is there anything else? Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I hate to -- I will be brief. But we just did receive a new updated witness list from the Prosecutor. And I think that's a good offer on their part, but if you go down to December 9th, 10th, 11th, and -- 9th, 10th, and 11th and the 19th, we have something that they list as spill-over VRS witnesses. I believe that that is insufficient notice for the Defence to be prepared for cross-examination of these witnesses. And we're only looking at two weeks away. We must be prepared. It's before the Christmas holiday. And just the term "spill-over VRS witnesses" is insufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe those are the protected witnesses. I'm not sure about it. Mr. McCloskey, could you shed some light on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that means that we don't anticipate being able to do two witnesses a day, as it's scheduled, because these are subpoena witnesses. We put them down for the dates that they are subpoenaed. I think, and as we've discussed with counsel before, we won't be able to do two witnesses a day. What spill-over means is the insurance time period to make up for witnesses that take too long. So I don't think we have any other witnesses in mind for that. I do -- there are another -- there are at least one other witness that I can think of that's on the list that we're still trying to figure out where we can put him in, but that's not meant to go into the spill-over. As soon as we figure out where to put that next witness in, we'll talk with counsel about it. But that is just purely meant as our rough estimate given the time frame that the Bratunac witnesses took, we are guessing that the Zvornik witnesses and the few new other Bratunac witnesses will take. That's all that means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You mean that you should leave sufficient time just in case you could not finish the previous witness. Thank you very much. Is there anything else that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Mr. Butler, do you have anything to say at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was reviewing last night's transcripts and I noted one error in the transcript that I wanted to correct before the final transcripts were done. It would be day 53 and the time is 12.14.49 and in the sentence there it says "the rear service company" and what should be in there is "elements of the rear service company".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also have to bear in mind that yesterday the communication between and Mr. Karnavas is just too fast. We should make it humanly possible to take every word of your testimony in the transcript. Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it my understanding we're only sitting until 12.00 today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe we were talking about the orders yesterday when we left off, the order with respect to -- the combat order of the Bratunac Brigade. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I just briefly want to go over it. Do you have it handy with you? It's been marked for identification purposes as P409.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that 406, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 406, yes. We're off to a bad start, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we received a new list of the documents you are going to use during the cross-examination. It seems to me that list keeps growing day by day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, Your Honour. Very well. I'll see what I can do about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, we talked -- yesterday we said that the order of July -- 5 July 1995 was slightly different than what was tasked of the Bratunac Brigade by the 2nd July order issued by the Drina Corps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you had indicated that something might have happened in between receiving that order and the order that was drafted by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. Isn't that correct? Or am I misstating your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That's generally correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Might that be an assumption on your part that there was a verbal or an oral communication by the Drina Corps to the Bratunac Brigade commander? Is that what you're relying on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In light of the fact we have no document which reflects that, I am assuming that it was an oral directive or an oral modification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it also be a modification of that order based on the commander's own interpretation of the order given to him and his assessment, his realistic assessment of what his brigade could actually do given the -- under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expect that would be the most probable reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That would be the most probable reason for him getting an oral modification, but what I'm saying is could the commander of the Bratunac Brigade on his own had decided to give his brigade a lesser role and still try to maintain within the spirit of the previous order, given his understanding of what his troops could realistically do under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could, but he would be expected to then inform the corps commander that his troops could not realistically achieve the goal that was set. So there would be some back and forth between the superior command on this, but that is what the commander would do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that is an assumption on your part, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We have no doubt on that one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And you're not discounting the commander of the Bratunac Brigade on his own, without even seeking permission from his commander, sought a lesser role for his brigade but within the context of what was mandated of him from the order that he had gotten?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we -- in fact, we discussed briefly how the Zvornik Brigade, Colonel Pandurevic, even on the very same day as the order that was drafted, or the order that he received from the Drina Corps, had drafted his own order in which it would appear that he has taken on, perhaps not a larger role, but he's going down there with more troops than the order originally envisaged. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did check that, and according to the preparatory order from the Drina Corps, Colonel Pandurevic was directed to assemble the equivalent of an infantry battalion. He did so. He brought with him some extra firepower with respect to the armour mechanised company and some artillery support, some very small artillery support. So it was certainly a very robust battalion. Whether that was the overall intent or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you could flip to the very last page of this order prepared by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, we will see, will we not, that there is a designation as to who was copied with this order, where this order was forwarded to. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it designates that there were six copies made and forwarded and it designates the various places. But we don't see any designation that a copy of this went to the Drina Corps commander, does it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Although one might make the assumption that they were handed a copy perhaps in Pribicevac which is where the Drina Corps had its forward command post during the attack on Srebrenica, that is an assumption we could make?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one possibility, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in looking at this order, it would appear, would it not, if we went down to each particular battalion, the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, and I'll stop there for now, it seemed that they had a defensive role to play. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. With the exception of the 3rd Battalion which had some limited offensive tasks assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then if we were to see -- there was -- the commander apparently had envisaged the place where the prisoners would be kept in the event they were -- his brigade came across prisoners, captured prisoners of war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, as I understand it, the prisoners normally when they are captured, they move backward from the battle line on backwards. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the general practice, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And normally they would move from backwards to upwards, in other words it goes to a higher command the further back they go. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The practice that was established by the VRS with this respect was that when a prisoner was captured, the commander of the units that captured him would have a limited time to interrogate the prisoner to obtain what we would call combat information. Once that was done, the prisoner was supposed to be evacuated back to the next higher level of command as rapidly as possible so additional information could be taken from the prisoner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after that collection point, perhaps go even further up to a bigger facility if the numbers became so large that their temporary holding facilities could not contain them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about facility, but it's a process that a prisoner moves up through various levels, and at each level he can be questioned with respect to the data that he might have that that next level would find to be of use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And in this particular case the commander of the Bratunac Brigade had designated Pribicevac, the forward command post, his forward command post, which was adjacent to the forward command post of the Drina Corps, as a storage place for prisoners of war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's the storage place, but at that point it is the first collection point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Collection point.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can assume, using the sort of logic that you have been using in your process, that the commander who was also there throughout that entire period wanted to be in close proximity to any prisoners captured. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In this respect it would make a great deal of sense to allow the information that the prisoners had that could be put to immediate use by the commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also to ensure full compliance with the Geneva Conventions as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because if the commander is there, he can ensure that they are properly cared for, fed, and they're not mistreated. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's proper command oversight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I understand it, throughout that period, at least until the fall of Srebrenica, no prisoners were captured by the Bratunac Brigade, unless I'm wrong?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no documents which reflect that prisoners were captured during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so can we conclude, since the commander was there on the battlefield or at the command post overseeing the situation, that his troops did not bring any prisoners back to Pribicevac, which was the collection point for prisoners where they would be questioned and kept until they moved further down or further up the line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't conclude that because the fact that prisoners aren't being reported as being captured in the daily combat reports. There is evidence that notes, although it's at a later period of time, that prisoners were being captured, and they're also not being reported. So I just can't make that conclusion. It is a logical assumption, but I can't conclude that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the terrain where the Bratunac Brigade was situated and that's where the static defence line had been and we look at the tasks that they were given, and then we add the fact that there was no real engagement between the Bratunac Brigade and the 28th Division, in fact there was -- it is my understanding that there was almost no engagement at all and then they leave Srebrenica. Would that also not -- those facts, would they not help us at least get us closer to an assumption we could rely on, that in all likelihood no prisoners were captured by the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a compound question. Several facts stated in there and then a question at the end of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll break it down, Your Honour. I assumed the gentleman wanted to go home on time. I'll break it down, take my time, fact by fact. I'll go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew where the static defence line was of the Bratunac Brigade, did you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have a rough idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, when you look at this particular order by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, in essence they were still at that static defence line, albeit they had been given some tasks along those lines. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know for a fact whether that defence line, whether the Bratunac Brigade, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th Battalion were ever attacked and came into contact with the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in the daily combat reports, with respect to the 1st and 4th Battalion during that period, in some of their reporting they indicate some minor skirmishing along their lines with the 28th Division. But again, the skirmishing, it's not significant contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not significant contact because they're not close enough to come across any prisoners of war. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular instance while they're still in their trench lines, I don't believe that prisoners were taken by those two units..

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wouldn't make sense, in fact. It wouldn't make, to quote one of your terms, military logic for the 28th to attack in that direction, given that at this point in time they were wondering what to do next?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would not make a lot of sense to launch a major attack in that particular direction, given the fact that they were facing a superior, at least in firepower, force in another direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And wouldn't that be a piece of information that would be helpful to synthesise into this analytical process that you have used throughout your investigative or your analytical period with the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a helpful piece of information, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when we synthesise that piece of information, along with the piece of information we talked about where they were located, and the fact that we don't have any prisoners in Pribicevac, can we then not come closer to the assumption that in all likelihood no prisoners were captured by the Bratunac Brigade between the 5th and 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it is an assumption. However, the fact is that I don't know one way or the other whether there were prisoners in Pribicevac. That is an open question which I do not have an answer to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So what you're saying is you didn't come across any documents, any daily reports, anything that would give you some inkling. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did come across some daily reports of the Bratunac Brigade throughout -- during that period, no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we have the entire selection of Bratunac Brigade daily reports through that period, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would not one expect that if a prisoner or prisoners were captured and put in Pribicevac where the commander was, that that information would be put in the daily report and forwarded up to the chain of command of the Drina Corps. Would one not expect -- would you not expect to see that in the daily combat report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect to see it, however keep in mind the process that during that period, most of the leadership, certainly with respect to the chief of staff and then by the 10th, the commanders, were there at Pribicevac. And for that to happen, he would also have to have that information transmitted from the Pribicevac headquarters down to the operations centre of the Bratunac Brigade, which was actually drafting the daily combat reports. To my knowledge, they were not drafted in Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And there was no means of communication between Pribicevac and Bratunac. Is that what you're telling me today, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I didn't say that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So they could have, given the communication means available, placed a call to inform them that we have a prisoner, so that whoever was responsible for preparing the daily report that would have to be sent at or around 1600 hours every day to the Drina Corps could make sure that that information was in the daily report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They could have. And in fact, in some of the reporting it is clear that they're receiving information from Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it a fact, sir, that we have sat here for an entire week, your direct examination, where you use these reports, selectively albeit, to establish that everything is working as the rules require, because you're piecing -- you're looking at one report and another document and you're drawing certain conclusions from them. Haven't you done this the first week on direct examination when you were being questioned by your colleague, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that that is true, that the system was working as designed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and we don't have anything in -- we don't have any combat daily reports from the Drina Corps that it would send up to the Main Staff that would reflect that any prisoners came from the Bratunac Brigade or were captured by the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do not have any Drina Corps combat reports or their daily reports prior to the period, I believe, 11 July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So we're handicapped there at least?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we just don't have any data on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And from your, it would make it about five years of investigation on this case, you have not come across any witnesses, have you, that would -- that have told you that we had X amount of number of war prisoners in Pribicevac that were captured by the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, no witnesses have indicated that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, in this report the commander of the Bratunac Brigade has designated that his military police will be his reserve. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, we're talking about on the average of 30 military police for the entire brigade as -- that's the number, 30 police, give or take one or two. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that number is roughly accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is that 30 when they're all on duty or is it -- are some of those off-duty on a rotation. Because after all, these were reservists, were they not, citizen soldiers, serving two weeks on, one week off, one month on, one month off?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may even be the entire end strength number. I just -- I'd have to go back and look at it. I don't have a number to throw out, but it was not a very large formation. The fact that it was serving one week on or one week off, again we're at a point in time where there was, supposedly after 16th June, 1995, a full mobilisation and everyone was supposed to be there an a full-time basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can assume that everyone was mobilised and that's a good assumption, at more or less full strength 30 military police.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could check the numbers, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Butler, am I not correct in stating that a certain number of military police were required to conduct day-to-day affairs for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you have a ballpark figure of how many -- what the number might be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect, the Bratunac Brigade MP log might be the most accurate barometer by which to measure that in the days up to or prior to 12 July where it lists the duty functions of the MPs and where they are. I think the ballpark number between the shift work and everything else is probably 10 to 12 with the various checkpoints and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So if we can agree on a figure of 30, and I know that you can go check it and you can do that at some point, and we can agree on another figure of 10, we're talking, realistically speaking, 20 MPs as the total reserve for the Bratunac Brigade during the attack on Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume that if the unit were to be assembled and thrown into a combat function, that a decision would be made to stop the police duty of the other 10 and send them or not, but still we're talking about a rather minuscule force of 20 to 30 military police as the reserve, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the size of the Bratunac Brigade at the time of the attack on the battlefield or the -- let me correct that, on the static defence line, albeit they had some offensive tasks as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Numbers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. Ballpark figure.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the number of 2.150 or so is the number that the Bratunac Brigade reports to the Drina Corps in their 4 July semi-annual report as their end strength, their total number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we use the assumption we did earlier, that is that full mobilisation, you could expect more or less all of them are going to be there, minus the ones that have -- are absent, because as you indicated that was a common problem that they would go AWOL, absent without leave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have those individuals who would not be present. You have individuals who would be sick who would not be present. So there are a lesser amount of numbers from the total end strength, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the total reserve for the Bratunac Brigade during the attack on Srebrenica was about 30 for 2.000. What do you make of that number?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very small reserve force and one that would not be capable of accomplishing very many missions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would that say, you know, this little scenario, what does it say of the Bratunac Brigade, its capabilities as a brigade itself on the field?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a comparative measure with standards --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking for comparative measure on standards. You see, I know how to ask that question. I'm asking you: Given what was going on, work with me today. Given what was going on, what do you make of that? You have 2.000 soldiers and you got 20 in reserve and there's a battle going on. In that scenario. I don't care how much the Milici Brigade has or the Zvornik Brigade has, that's not my concern. I'm concerned about the Bratunac Brigade in this situation. What does it tell us? And you're the military analyst.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In isolation, what you have then is a unit that is in rather poor shape with respect to the ability to conduct combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, those numbers didn't change during -- the numbers with respect to the military police did not change over the days, that is, after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That remained the same?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, to my knowledge, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we were to go from there to -- I don't want to get ahead of myself too much, but just since we're on the military police, once Srebrenica falls and you have all these, for lack of a better term, VIP, executive officers, coming into Bratunac, as I understand it one of the missions for the military police is to provide security for them. Is that correct? Not all of them, but some of them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you know who was there and you know what was going on, so help me out. Mladic, General Mladic, he would require a few MPs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By this point they have guests, the DutchBat, who are at Hotel Fontana. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even though it is a rather comfortable or was a comfortable hotel, nonetheless they need security, both to make sure that nothing happens to them and I would suspect to make sure that they don't wander off, because in all likelihood they would be viewed as a bargaining chip, correct, and in fact I believe they were at one point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There would have been a military police requirement to provide security for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any numbers as to how many were required for that mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe while the mission is noted in the military police log, I don't know if there's a number associated offhand, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you had indicated that you believed that on the average of 10 to 12 every day for their general everyday activities, did that figure include providing security for the DutchBat at Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That would have been -- that would be an excess requirement, not an anticipated one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it if I were to ask you about the security for General Mladic, the answer would be the same?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they need to provide any security for General Krstic, after all he is the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect that General Krstic would have his own security, and in fact, I understand from his testimony in the last case that he did at least have one of his own security people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mladic had his own security people, too -- or I guess his close protection unit, CPUs, as you probably know them. But in addition to his own close protection unit, he also had an entourage, if I could use that word, of military police from the Bratunac Brigade, who apparently travelled around as Mladic went about his way during those days. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He was escorted by the Bratunac military police in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So now if you could, if you could help us out here, and again I think we fixed on a number of 30 or maybe slightly more, but we'll stay -- for the sake of consistency, let's stay with 30. If we had 30 known military police, and let's say everybody was healthy and had reported and was on duty, when we take the 12 -- 10 that are required, we'll stay at a low number, that were required on a day-to-day basis to carry out their normal functions. And then we add the security for the DutchBat and the security for General Mladic and whoever else may need security, could you tell us approximately how many military police would the Bratunac Brigade have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have a time period for this specific question. Because there's periods where Mladic and Krstic are gone during these days, so it may be more valuable if it was more specific to dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's reasonable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the period of the 11th to the period of the -- say the 17th. Could you give me that or do you want to go day by day? You pick. It doesn't matter to me.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to note that the requirement would change by the afternoon or early evening hours of the 13th of July when both General Mladic and General Krstic are no longer in the Bratunac Brigade area. So that would be a major shift. The other functions should, in theory, remain the same. So while I'm not sure I want to speculate on a ballpark number, there should in the abstract be more military police available by the later hours of 13 July, because those that were assigned to the security of General Mladic would have presumably been released from that task when we departed the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say presumably when some have, I think there's been testimony here, that they've gone as far as Han Pijesak with him. That's where his headquarters is, no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is. And again I'm assuming that once he arrives that there at a point in time they would be released and returned back to the Bratunac Brigade zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Han Pijesak from Bratunac? How long would it take to get there during that period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending, again, on the road situation, at least a few hours during the day and I suspect that if it was during the evening, the military police may well have spent the evening there because the road was probably too dangerous to travel at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the picture you've painted for us doesn't really change that dramatically until perhaps the 14th, mid-morning or early morning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I don't know the window. I don't want to indicate a time, because obviously we don't know facts in this instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Mladic did come back into the area, I believe, on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that General Mladic from the late afternoon or early evening of the 14th July and through the 15th of July was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know on the 14th he was. But we do have testimony -- we do have a statement, do we not -- maybe I'm getting my days mixed. But we do have a statement from the chief of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade who indicated that, in his statement to OTP when he testified, that Mladic ordered him and Popovic to escort a convoy of prisoners into the Zvornik area. Do you recall reading that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I've read that. The issue that I'm recalling is that during the Krstic trial, and I assume it has been one of the exhibits that has been forwarded through as part of all that, is an affidavit from a British Major General Elliot who was a military advisor to Mr. Bildt who places General Mladic in Belgrade on the evening of the 14th and in meetings of the 15th. So that's the piece of information that I'm working off of the location of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course the piece of information I'm working off of is a piece of information that came into your possession - your, the Prosecution's possession - after the Krstic trial. But in any event --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it was during the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The affidavit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about what I'm referring to. I'm referring to fresher information. In any event --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that context, and again, yes, sir, even in General Krstic's own testimony, he makes the testimony that General Mladic is with him at the IKM in Krivace on the morning of 15 July 1995. So there are conflicting reports, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now that we've settled that. You can even discount how many military police would have been with General Mladic. We still have the DutchBat, do we not, up to a certain point, guests of the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the DutchBat people from the Hotel Fontana are evacuated to the FRY sometime during the 15th, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So could you give us a ballpark figure now. Take out what would be -- what would have been required for General Krstic and tell me what would be the ballpark figure.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are using the number of 30, I suspect the number of military police available for other duties, the high end number would be 15 and it would probably be even less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say -- are we talking out the 10 that we talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm subtracting the 10 that are doing routine duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now you have 20, so you're saying from then you probably need 5 or so, so now we're down to about 15. But of course you had some wounded folks at the hospital, did they not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I understand there was a military police presence there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So we're talking relatively 10 to 15, as a high number, military police available for other duties during that period. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean that takes into account other variables that I don't know which would be when the military police or if the military police abandoned the Zuti Most checkpoint because it no longer needed to be garrisoned, things of that nature. But yeah, 10 to 15 is a good number, sir, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, now, the next stop we're going to be speaking about is Potocari. But before we get there, I want to run through some of these orders since we started with the orders to see what the Bratunac Brigade was tasked to do during this period. As I understand it, after this -- after the fall of Srebrenica, the next order in essence we have for the Bratunac Brigade is to send a company towards Zepa. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking only the written order, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the written orders. You're assuming now - that's an assumption on your part - that they are oral orders, right? Is that an assumption?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of the interviews, and we discussed this interview yesterday, the battalion commanders indicate, at least the 2nd Battalion commander indicates that they were instructed to move from their positions and to occupy the positions of the former -- that the 28th Division had formerly held. So there was some limited orders given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're assuming that that gentleman is correct, right, and that the other one is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not an either/or situation, I try to look at every piece of information and see where it fits in context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I don't want to fight yesterday's battle but I got plenty of energy today. Now, yesterday, you said that one gentleman said that he had received the order and his commander said, "I'm unaware of that, maybe the deputy commander might have given him an order, but as far as I know he wasn't given any orders." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the piece I'm talking about, but I can explain. The deputy battalion commander at that time -- or the acting battalion commander noted that on the morning of the 12th he was instructed that the companies were to move out of their positions, and as he notes, to occupy the positions of the former 28th Infantry Division. It has nothing to do with the next step whether they were ordered to go to Potocari or not. I see no reason to believe that that would not be a logical order to give.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The next order that we have that was handed down, I believe, by General Zivanovic, was that -- was it not to -- for the Bratunac Brigade to assemble a sizeable company to send towards Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The order by General Zivanovic, if we're referring to the 13 July orders where the retransmission of -- or the -- essentially the reiteration of a Main Staff order with respect to activities related to the column. The one that you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- On the company was the one that was published afterwards by General Krstic while he was still the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct. So we have -- which order came first, by the way, Zivanovic's or Krstic's?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to go back and look at the time stamps. I don't know the answer to that offhand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm referring to what has been marked for identification purposes as, I believe, 468/A, and then while you're at it, if you could pull out 467/A. Then I wanted to talk about the other 13th July order. And this one is -- I believe it's 472/A. Sir, I wanted to talk about those written orders on July 13 just very briefly. No drama. If you could look at those orders, because I'm trying -- I would like at least since we have these documents to try to get a time frame on how things are evolving, at least with respect to the Bratunac Brigade, in light of everything else that's going on. Okay. So which order comes first on the 13th, sir? And incidentally, before you answer that question, we don't have another written order before that for the 12th or the 11th, do we? I mean, I don't know. You would.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, from the Drina Corps to the Bratunac Brigade, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are a series of orders by General Zivanovic with respect to orders for the subordinate brigade formations to assemble buses and have them sent to Bratunac. And the other one which is specific to the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigade, which one directs the Zvornik Brigade to send a military police detachment to Konjevic Polje and the other one directs the Bratunac Brigade to work with, and I don't know the exact word there, that may be an issue so we'll leave it for the document, with the Bratunac municipal police for providing security along the Bratunac/Konjevic Polje road. So those orders are issued on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And is there anything nefarious, if I could use that word, about those orders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at face value, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now we get to the 13th -- and by the way, those orders did not require -- were not directed towards the battalions or were they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were directed to the brigade commands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The brigade command, but the orders require the usage of the battalions within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to providing for transport. I mean, whether it was decided to go to the battalions and pull any vehicles they may have had or not, I mean, that's speculative. I don't know the answer to that. It's certainly not directly to the battalions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the orders don't require the commander to pull off any troops from the line --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not specified to do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now we get to the 13th. Now, on the 13th which order comes first?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue in trying to determine that is that of the three, Prosecution Exhibit 468, which is the Krivaja forward command post order signed by the chief of staff does not have a stamp on it which would indicate when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My, again, assessment on this is given the fact that it is still signed by General Krstic as the chief of staff as opposed to corps commander indicates that it was sent prior to between 18 and 2000 hours during the period he assumed command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecution Exhibit 467, which is the 13 July order with respect to preventing passage of Muslim groups to Tuzla signed by General Zivanovic as the commander indicates that it was sent out at 1720 hours on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So from that -- well, can you conclude which one came first, because I thought you said when I mentioned one you said -- you corrected me. Can you determine which one came first?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this instance I can't determine which one came first because I do have no way of knowing. I can tell you with respect to the Krivaja 0714 order, which is Prosecution 468, it would have been sent no later than, because of the reference to General Krstic as the chief of staff. But I can't say how much earlier it was sent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What if we were to use military logic, which of the two would you expect to come first? Or it's totally different and you couldn't speculate or you could not look at them and make any conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that looking at the actual internals of the order that the order from General Zivanovic, which was Prosecution 467, probably originated first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And that's 467?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I thought that was the one that I had started with, I might be wrong, but isn't that the one that requested a company or so be assembled by -- I might be wrong --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What you're referring to is a directive in Prosecution Exhibit 468.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So what is General Zivanovic requesting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this one, the first one which is Prosecution 467, General Zivanovic is directing or giving a series of orders to the brigade commands in their areas of responsibilities, and it lists seven or eight specified tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In essence, what is the essence of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he is directing is that the brigade commands take the steps necessary, all measures necessary, to block, disarm, and capture the Muslim groups observed and preventing them crossing into Muslim territory. I think the first paragraph or the first order in that encapsulates the other ones. There are some other functions that are a part of that, but I think that's the big picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he order the Bratunac Brigade to advance in any way, in other words to chase after the column that's on its way towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. It's not specified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then we have the next order from General Krstic. What order was that -- was does that order say, that's 468?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that call for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 468 calls for -- with respect to just the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It calls for them to form one company and, I think I can put it specifically on the ELMO, if that's what you want, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could do that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 7 or paragraph 5/7 specifies that task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what is that task?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to allocate one company to join the Milici Light Infantry Brigade and carry out the tasks assigned to the Milici Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so now we're reducing the Bratunac Brigade in size a little bit more, not by much, but --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's your understanding that based on this order, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade did, in fact, act on it, and in fact, I believe it was the chief of staff that led that company. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, both the size of the company and the individual directing it were specified in what is, I believe, an interim combat report for the 13th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any -- have you drawn any conclusion as to why the chief of staff might have been assigned to that task and not just some lower level commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I've drawn no conclusions on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you in your mind think about it at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have actually thought about it a lot, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I was just wondering. All right. And then there's another order on the same day, on the 13th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now we've got a third order to the Bratunac Brigade, and what does this order call for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular order is Prosecution 472, is the order to the Bratunac Brigade, Skelani Separate Battalion and Milici Brigade to mount active [sic] search operations or to search the terrain along various axes -- along various different axes in order to search the terrain through the former enclave area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say "mount active" --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said mount axis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were coming on different axis of advance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't hear you. I just thought -- I notice this time you said the word "search," when you normally like to use the word "sweep". I think it's about time for the break, but if you can answer that very shortly, fine. If not, we can leave it -- well, we could leave it for after the break if you like.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "search" and it specifies "search". That's a fair translation, as far as I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there are other times, sir, when the document says search and you interject the term "sweep"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I discuss the term "sweep," it's my own understanding and that's again maybe a transference of my own Western terminology. Again, I try to be as true to the document and its terminology as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the searching that we're talking about here is sweeping, are we not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my mind what we're talking about in a Western term is that we are sweeping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this might be a good point if the Court so desires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Butler, I believe that we agreed on 13th July 1995 an order was issued by the now new commander as it would appear from this particular document for the Bratunac Brigade along with others to conduct a sweep operation. Correct, to use the terminology that you have been using on cross or direct examination?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it says "search". I've seen it alternatively translated as "combed". But translating it to my Western terminology, they're conducting a sweep operation or they've been directed to conduct a sweep operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I understand it, we agreed that a sweep operation is a proper military function, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's a normal military function. There's nothing sinister or nefarious about conducting one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact not only is it normal, it is one that would be expected after a particular battle. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, you would expect that such an order should have been issued. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean this is consistent with what should have been happening on the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it you have had an opportunity to look at the map and to plug the coordinates or at least get a ballpark figure of where the search or the sweeping of the terrain was to occur. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to this specific order, not in broad terms. We did that more with the Bratunac Brigade's order, which was the one that follows on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And we're going to get to that. But if we were to look at the map that we had yesterday, it would appear, would it not, that the area that at least General Krstic is ordering to be swept is one area which does indeed require sweeping?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could look at the -- what the commander of the Bratunac Brigade does based on the order that has been given to him by his commander or his superior, we see a rather detailed, do we not, order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this particular order, we see at least the 1st, the 2nd, and the 3rd Battalions are given rather detailed coordinates. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about a different document here. I don't have that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the trig points. I'm talking about the --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still have the Drina Corps order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I truly apologise. We've now moved on to the 14th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's an assumption on my part because I have my documents here I assume that I asked you to -- if we could go to what has been mark as P483. I have an extra copy --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise again. If you could take a look at it. Now, would it not appear that the 1st, the 2nd, and the 3rd Battalion are given rather detailed coordinates on the map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They are given detailed boundaries to conduct their operations in. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to take the map and to try to plot them out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we did that several years and that was a component of my testimony in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when plotting out these points, did you find anything sinister or nefarious about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Infantry Battalions, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, the order that was issued by the Bratunac Brigade commander was consistent with the order given to him and consistent with the terrain requirements at the time, that is that particular terrain that needed to be swept. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then when we get to the 4th Infantry Battalion, there may be an issue as to the interpretation of one word. I don't know if you're aware of that. The word "spreading." It says: "From its position, the 4th Infantry Battalion will control the area in front of it spreading from," and there may be some room for interpretation on that particular word. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I wasn't aware that that was an issue in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it your understanding -- is it your understanding that -- well, what is your understanding of controlling the area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I leave that as an interpretation issue. Controlling the area could imply physically having your forces on the ground. There is another interpretation that is controlling an area could be controlling it through the use of fire. So it is open to multiple interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And based on that order that was issued by Colonel Blagojevic with respect to this particular battalion, this aspect of the order is -- it is not sinister or nefarious in any way, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insomuch as the order, it's -- the issue of course is that the -- it is a known fact that Bosnian Muslim prisoners were being assembled at the meadow in Sandici, and this is a form of linkage. And again the answer is how far the forces moved forward with respect to controlling it and then they would come across what was then a crime scene at Sandici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The order itself, what I'm asking you to look at, and in light of the situation on the ground. And before you answer the question, let's go over the facts. The 28th Division was a fairly large force, at least numerically speaking. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe we discussed the number yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now they are going through RS territory, are they not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Once they leave the enclave, they are in the territory of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact they do pose somewhat, if I could borrow your term, a significant danger to the RS, do they not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, had they taken perhaps a different option, they may have even captured Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so this force, and incidentally at that time the RS, albeit it's after the 12th and the 13th, at that time the RS or the VRS was still not certain as to the actual strength and capabilities of this column. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that they became fully aware of it until, at best, the late evening of the 13th of July. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even then, it would appear that at least the upper echelon is rather indifferent to the pleas of Obrenovic or totally blind to the situation, because at least in the testimony of Colonel Obrenovic he indicated that when he was asking for help even on the 14th, the answers that he was getting seemed to be that the folks at the higher up had actually no clue of what was happening in his area. Do you recall reading that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And I believe, again going to some of the intercepts on the 14th, that you see are indicated again, that the senior leadership or senior officers still don't understand the gravity of the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So in light of all of what is happening on the ground and keeping in mind the limited information that is known and keeping the order that was given to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, when we dissect and analyse and synthesise this order the 14th that was prepared by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade and we look at what tasks are given to him, to the -- are given to the 4th Infantry Battalion, can we not conclude that those tasks are reasoned and proper, militarily?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So nothing sinister, nothing nefarious?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Other than just the association at Sandici, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you say association. Are you assuming that it was the Bratunac Brigade that committed atrocities in Sandici?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I just want to make sure that there's no subliminal messages being sent. All right. Now, if we could go to the 15th of July and on this -- what I want to focus your attention on is the proposal that was prepared by, as is commonly referred to these days, as the late Colonel Milanovic, because I believe he's no longer with us. He's passed away. Now, in your testimony I would like to -- well, first let's talk about this: It appears as if he has been tasked by his commander to make an assessment. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So based on his assessment, and I would imagine that he had to go around, get a lay of the land and see what everybody was doing, he then makes a proposal to his commander. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we get to the proposal, there is a section where he says: I have ordered. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, maybe I'm wrong. Maybe I'm wrong, but when we look at number 4, it would appear that he has ordered somebody from the Bratunac Brigade -- or am I incorrect in reading that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That's a correct interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so is he ordering the entire brigade or is he ordering the 1st Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade or do you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It specifically says that he has ordered -- that the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade to continue searching the terrain, clearing the battlefield in the direction of Bratunac/Konjevic Polje/Kasaba, and also to create some sort of reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was Colonel Milanovic's, what was his position in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His normal function was the chief of air defence, or anti-aircraft -- PDO, essentially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
