utterances.text: And we don't have any anti-aircraft activity going on, do we, at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arguably speaking, given the fact that there's still a concern about NATO bombing, there should have been a concern. But there's no active anti-aircraft activity going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer is no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where is he in the order, if you're looking at the staff of the Drina Corps? You've got the commander, you've got the chief of staff who was also the deputy commander, or acting commander when he's filling in, and then who would come after that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that would be Colonel Obrad Vicic is the chief of operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Chief of operations. Where does this fellow fit into the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a member of what is known as the corps -- he's part of the operative staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But he's not the number 2, and he's certainly not the number 3. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it appears that here he is giving direct orders to the brigade. Now, is that a violation of the unity of command principle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the context of the orders that he's giving, I believe that the inference could be drawn, and the proper inference is the orders that he's giving are in effect on the delegated authority of the corps commander. I mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The corps commander told him to make an assessment. He didn't say go order people around?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that Colonel Milanovic is informing the corps commander what orders that he's given, the fact that he states that he's given them as orders is to me an inference that the orders he's given in this respect are in conjunction or in line with the directives of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's an assumption that you're making. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Looking at it the next step down, he's very clear on what he can order or what he believes he has the authority to order and what things he has to propose for approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's when we get to the proposal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the proposal in essence is that since there's nobody else available to do a particular job that is required that he proposes that there be -- the appointment of the commander of the Bratunac Brigade to coordinate and to command this particular -- or to execute this particular proposal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Paragraph 1, it states that: "To authorise and appoint the commander of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade as the commander of all forces which participating in searching the terrain and sweeping the battlefields of the east of the road." And it specifies from there that they have no one available to appoint from the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is another sweeping operation or searching operation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is just a continuation of the one that's already in place, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The one you mean of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade was conducting its operation on the 14th, but in the broader context, other units that were along the road to Konjevic Polje and then down towards Milici were conducting similar operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in fact, the same order from General Krstic on the 13th gives tasks to the Milici Brigade as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, if we follow an earlier conclusion, nothing is requested in this proposal of the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, should he be appointed to do anything that is militarily improper under the circumstances. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe that's very correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just a minor point, a minor point of clarification. When you testified you were asked a series of questions with respect to this particular proposal, and I would like to invite your attention to your specific answer to that. So if we could have some assistance here. I want to go to page 4529 -- I'm sorry. 4529 and I will be referring to, actually it will be 4530 and 31. But at first if you could just look at this. This is from the official transcript or the corrected transcript dated Thursday, 13 November 2003. If you see on line 4, it refers to Exhibit 495, which I believe was the exhibit we were just discussing. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so now if you could go to the following page and look at -- this would be page 4530. And if we could look at line 17, there is a question posed to you on direct. And I'll read. It says: "Now, Mr. Butler, it appears that this proposal he has volunteered Mr. Blagojevic to command all these units and he has done it apparently from the Bratunac Brigade. Can you -- what can you conclude if anything about that?" And here is your answer: "Well, with respect to that individual piece, from a military perspective I have to presume," I'm underscoring that, "I have to presume that Colonel Milanovic discussed the issue with Mr. Blagojevic before recommending him for the task." Follow-up question: "Why is that?" Answer, this is line 25, we're about to go into the next page: "It would be very unusual and it certainly wouldn't be the proper function of a staff officer to make a recommendation or a proposal that subsequently would not be able to be carried out. As a matter of military professionalism on the part of the staff -- of staff officers, you don't make proposals that you know aren't going to be able to be executed. So as a matter of military common sense, as you will, one would not expect Colonel Milanovic to make this proposal if he did not already believe that Colonel Blagojevic would agree to the proposal or would be incapable of carrying out." Do you recall being asked those questions and giving those answers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before -- I just want to discuss some portions before I show you another document and ask your comments on it. But first of all, towards the end. It's not up to Colonel Blagojevic to agree with a proposal like that. Colonel Milanovic doesn't need to get Colonel Blagojevic's agreement. Correct? Because if his commander, General Krstic, gives him an order, a proper order such as this one, even if it might be somewhat a difficult task, basically he has to salute him and go about trying to carry out the order. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an abstract, yeah, that's how superior command works, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, it's not a debating society where they debate, "Well, maybe I'll do this, maybe I'll do that". The commander gives an officer, it's expected that the lower officer will do it. So that part of your answer isn't very helpful, is it? I could be much more caustic, but that's the best I can do. I'm trying to sugar-coat it today.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that with the fact that I disagree and what I would say is that in keeping with the functions of the staff officer as they are outlined, again, in the 1983 staff regulations, part of a staff officer's function is to be able to provide to his commander realistic possibilities, realistic plans for their approval. From a matter of military professionalism, as a staff officer, it would be hard for me to believe to Colonel Milanovic would have taken up the time and effort to make proposals to his corps commander as to the best way to accomplish what was rapidly becoming a very difficult mission without, at least in his own mind, understanding the options that he was proposing were feasible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But now we're going to the feasibility aspect. And I would agree with you to some extent on that, because you can't ask the impossible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas is again referencing his own personal viewpoints and agreements, which is not relevant, is not appropriate, and it tends to ratchet up the argumentative -- potential for argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, whether the testimony of this witness is helpful or not is the conclusion arrived by the Judges, not by you. Of course, during the cross-examination there are many, many occasions that you do not agree with the testimony of this witness. But just show your case to rebut whatever the witness said, rather than jump to the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked him about whether a lower officer would have to give his agreement. He went on to explain the latter part of that -- of his answer or would be incapable of carrying it out. Now, I could have done one of two things, one, act like Mr. McCloskey and be rude and stop him or let him go and then agree with him, the latter part is something that you would expect. He's not going to make a silly proposal that can't be carried out. I agree with him. That wasn't part of my question. My question was for the first part and it was a nicer way of trying to guide the witness back to the question that I had asked, as opposed to saying that's not what I asked and try to be aggressive. I'm trying a different tactic, Your Honour, but very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, try to put your question in a sugar-coated way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, would you not, that they don't need Colonel Blagojevic's agreement. It would be nice, but they don't need his agreement, do they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They don't need his agreement, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I said that part of your answer is not very helpful, is it? It doesn't make sense, in other words, militarily speaking, because if we're going to apply military logic, a military common sense, your terms, even military professionalism, when a higher officer gives an order, he doesn't need the agreement of the lower officer, even if he's asking the lower officer to do something that may seem rather impossible. Isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, not only do I agree, but I believe that you're forgetting the context under which this document was drafted. In this particular case at the direction of the corps commander, Colonel Milanovic went out, he visited these units, he discuss the situation or he learned the situation, and it is a component of his proposal to the corps commander, he was the one who proposed that Colonel Blagojevic should be appointed in command and he specified that the proposal was made because there were no other available Drina Corps officers. That is in my mind, and again using all of the various logic and common sense barometers that I know of, that is a proper and appropriate function of what a staff officer should be doing with respect to offering realistic proposals to his commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But it was -- but I guess what I'm having some difficulty is with your assumption or presumption here that he would have discussed this matter with Colonel Blagojevic at the time. That's just a guess on your part, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have caveated that as a presumption, yes, sir. And I believe I have explained why I have caveated it as a presumption. I don't believe that Colonel Milanovic, if he was doing his job conscientiously and attempting to give, at that time, General Krstic the best available proposal that he would have made a proposal for Colonel Blagojevic to assume command of those units if he knew that there were circumstances that would preclude the successful accomplishment of that function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And one of them was not whether Mr. Blagojevic would have agreed or disagreed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the conversation, if in fact one had occurred, would have been less along the lines of agreement or disagreement and more along the lines of: "Are you capable of carrying out the mission if it's given to you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you, just as an aside, what has been marked as P466/A. Just to show you an -- I have a copy. I believe you recognise this order and I believe you've already commented on it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this comes from Lieutenant General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is he from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant General Gvero, or it should be Lieutenant Colonel General Gvero, at that time was the assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs from the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And it would appear he is a staff officer, is he not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is an assistant commander, yes, sir. It's not a staff officer at that level. He is the assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here he's not the number 2 at the Main Staff, is he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, he is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he the number 3?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the general staff hierarchy, given the absence of Colonel Milovanovic -- or Colonel General Milovanovic, it should have been General Major Miletic with respect to operational issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer is no? He's not the number 3.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer for that for all purposes. I just know for operational issues it should be General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you even stated that during that period of time at some point he was filling in as the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He was listed as the acting chief of staff of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this order, we seem to see a staff officer or an assistant commander from the Main Staff giving orders all the way down to the brigades. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so -- the order is not going to the commander of the Drina Corps and then for him to give those orders, but it would appear that here we have an aberration, do we not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is not the normal way that it occurs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And my point being, we really can't make these broad generalisations, such as the one that you made with respect to Milanovic, that obviously or presumably he would have spoken to Mr. Blagojevic because of X, Y, and Z, because there seem to be quite a few aberrations in this particular army at this particular time given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. He has called Mr. Butler's answer a broad generalisation, which is argumentative and is actually, I think, a misstatement of Mr. Butler's more specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you'll have to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see one aberration, rather visible. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So we can accept that. And so what my point is: Given -- this is just one example by which we can conclude that we just can't make presumptions in this case that things are always done by the book, can we?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what this document has to do with that point insomuch as when this document is discussed with other individuals that, while they note that it's an aberration, they also note that it is not an uncommon occurrence. Now, getting back to your question --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I did in fact say it was a presumption on my part. I clearly don't have facts which say a conversation did or did not occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you go on to state, sir, and this is where I have some problems --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. He's interjecting he has personal problems with the witness. It is argumentative and if it goes on and on it will eventually end in chaos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, in this question, I did not see any problems. Maybe Mr. Karnavas has not finished his question yet. Would you please move on, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then state, however, it would be very unusual and it certainly wouldn't be proper, proper function of a staff officer to make recommendations or proposals that subsequently would not be able to be carried out and as a matter of military professionalism on that part of staff officers, you don't make proposals and so and so forth. So here you seem to be not making merely a presumption, but then you're saying that it would be very unusual. In other words, are you not, sir, trying to have us come to the conclusion that in all likelihood, there must have been communication and perhaps even approval by Mr. Blagojevic. Isn't that what you're trying to get us to conclude, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to forward before the Court in this matter is that if Colonel Milanovic was diligently conducting his functions as a staff officer with the background that he had and with the knowledge that he had, and had he been doing it the way it was supposed to be done as envisioned in the rules and regulations, that that should have occurred. I can't say that it did and I cannot say that it didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. I accept that answer, and as I've indicated by showing you P466, we saw one rather major aberration from someone who you would expect to know the rules and to apply them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well again, sir, with respect to P466, the answer that we hear when we discuss this issue with VRS officers is that, one, it is addressed to the command of the Drina Corps. And if it's directly addressed to some of the subordinate brigades, the practical aspect is that this is a message that the higher-ups wanted to ensure that the people heard and everyone heard it at the same time and in a hurry. It's not necessarily an aberration with that respect. I mean, it's a military necessity issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So now you're backtracking from your initial position? It sounds like you're back-pedalling, Mr. Butler. Is that because I've been able to show you proof that by making these presumptions, sometimes you may reach the wrong conclusion, might that be the reason why you're back-pedalling right now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I suspect that you think I'm back-pedalling because that's what you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the 16th. Now, on the 16th, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade was given another order, was he not? Or was it on the 15th? Was he not to mobilise to go off to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That's the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I said, on the 16th he was given another order. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So if we look at what Milanovic has done, he's made a proposal. And if we look at the date, that's on the 15th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that going back, and I guess it's Prosecution Exhibit 495, the sent stamp is at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So that means that's when he sent it out. And can you draw any conclusions? Can you make any presumptions on this as far as when the approval would have come and when the next order would have been issued?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect, all I can go back to is that in his own testimony, General Krstic acknowledged receiving this and acknowledging that he did agree to the proposal. I don't believe that a time issue was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But then it seems almost immediately thereafter, maybe that's an overexaggeration, but we're talking about the 16th, the next day, the day that he's supposed to be carrying out these proposals, he's given another task, and that is to mobilise to leave the area and to go on another military campaign. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's given the task to assemble one infantry battalion to be prepared to deploy to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what might that entail?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's specified in the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. But what I'm saying is you from the military standpoint, what would it require from a commander's point of view? What does he need to do? Can he just issue an order and then relax and kick back and assume that it's been done or does he need to get actively involved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, presuming the process works as it's supposed to, what should happen is the commander will, of course, notify his staff and the affected battalion commander. The staff will begin to work on the various things that need to occur in order to make this happen. They will begin to assemble the transport. They will begin to ensure that all of the combat sets of ammunition, weapons, supplies, rations, all of that will be assembled and in the proper place. The battalion commander will have to engage in the process of stopping what military operation he's in then, withdrawing his forces from the field, doing some rest in whatever refit might be necessary, have them at the proper place at the proper time to embark on the vehicles. While at face value it appears to be simple, certainly behind every military order there is a variety of implied tasks that have to happen by a lot of people in order to make these functions occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would that require the commander's oversight, and keep in mind that the chief of staff is gone, he's already down in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is something that as an order the commander should oversee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could show you what has been marked for identification purposes P497, it might give us some inkling from which to work back on. If we could go to the July 16, 1995. Have you seen this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would seem, would it not, that as early as 0700 hours, it says here -- I'm sorry it says that the formation of the battalion to Zepa -- I guess by 0700 hours on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is consistent with the written order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so this may not -- this could not necessarily give us any indication as to whether Colonel Blagojevic had received the order for Zepa early on the 16th or later during the day on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. To my knowledge there's no indication associated when this order was received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, before receiving this order for Zepa, as I understand it, we have some documentation, do we not, where the commander in a rather detailed fashion indicated who would be transferred to the Trnovo -- to Trnovo where they had their mandatory obligation. I guess every month or so they would send a certain amount of troops, and the ones that were there would come back. Do you recall what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you're referring to a 15 July order which sets up a rotation at the Trnovo front. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rotation. That was the word that didn't come to mind. So that rotation was coming up, and in fact if we look at that order it would seem that it would take some diligence and some precision to ensure that the right mixture of people were sent down. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that -- did that rotation occur, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it occurred on schedule, because some of the records that we have from the 4th Drinski Brigade, which was in fact -- Bratunac was part of that unit or the Bratunac rotation was part of that unit indicate that the shift had been delayed. It may have taken place at a later point in time. I just don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might the new campaign towards Zepa been one of the reasons for that shift delay?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and it would be the most logical reason -- or not necessarily the new campaign. It's the engagement of the Bratunac Brigade forces to replace those from the Zvornik Brigade that had been pulled out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact if we were to look at the July 16 order by Colonel Blagojevic at P498 on paragraph 7, it does state, I believe, members of the 1st Infantry Battalion who were scheduled to replace troops in Trnovo on 20 July 1995 will be included in the formation of the 1st Infantry Battalion. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And of course if we look at, again at P497, it is the 1st Battalion that's going to go down there in full strength. And in fact I believe you've already testified to, it's going to be led by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no order that specifies that it's going to be led by the commander, but in fact our understanding through the intercepts is that the brigade commander did accompany that formation down on 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So -- all right. In other words, he could have sent somebody else to command his troops, instead the commander went with his troops. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular instance, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which may also help us understand why perhaps the commander, when he sent the company on the 13th to Zepa that was going to be attached to another unit to fight a campaign down there, send his chief of staff to make sure that his troops were properly cared for and not put in harm's way unnecessarily by some other reckless -- by some reckless commander or someone who might wish to place the Bratunac Brigade soldiers in a situation where others would not wish to be in.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's why I asked you whether you had considered that as a possibility in the mix as to why Colonel Blagojevic sends his chief of staff in the middle of these activities down there. Now, if we look at what has been marked as P539, I believe. It is the 17th July -- I apologise to Madam Usher for all the traffic. If we look at this, this is the -- dated July 17th, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it appears that it is sent very urgent and it is an order from none other than the commander of the VRS, General Mladic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this order, it would appear, would it not, that the Main Staff, not the corps but the Main Staff is ordering all the way down to the brigade that a search operation take place. Correct? At least in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe that it's just -- what they're ordering is that a Main Staff officer will take over the search operation that has been continuing. It's not a new operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification, but that's exactly my point. This is just a continuation of the sweeping of the terrain, which you have already indicated was a proper military function in that particular area at that point in time, given the circumstances. Now, Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic, where is he from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic is a Main Staff officer. He is from the security branch, so he's from the intelligence and security administration. And by function his job is oversight of the military police of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I'm not mistaken, if I'm not mistaken, you have indicated at least for this limited task, this order, those who are under the command and control, those who are -- that Keserovic is directing are under his command and control or the Main Staff's command and control. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those individuals or those components of the units that are conducting the sweep operation and that are under his direction are, in effect, under his command. He controls them and he is a Main Staff officer. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So -- because I believe the question came from the Prosecution whether this was an -- whether the Main Staff was effectively taking over the brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, and your answer was: "No. They're not exercising total control and command over the brigade," but in this particular order for this particular period, for these particular tasks they are no longer under the command and control of the Bratunac Brigade commander, but rather under the command and control of the Main Staff, and in particular, Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, yes, Colonel Keserovic does not take over control of the brigade or command of the brigade but he is put in charge of or he's placed in control of those forces that are engaged in the sweep operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you considered or done any thinking as to why would General Mladic at this point intervene. Do you have an answer for us on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that, given the fact that Colonel Blagojevic had deployed with his forces, and I will take one step and say that I assume if Colonel Blagojevic deployed to Zepa he did so with the direction of General Krstic, considering that took out the person who was controlling these operations prior and that there were no suitable officers at the Drina Corps, given the engagements, that the Drina Corps had either requested or the Main Staff directed that they had to appoint an officer to take control of this. In the context of the overall military situation, they were rapidly running out of qualified people to command formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we trace this back only two days earlier, you had the assistant commander for anti-aircraft activity making a proposal. And we can assume that General Krstic, the commander then, made an order. At the same time, the same commander orders, slightly thereafter, for the commander to leave and engage himself in a military campaign for which will take the part of a better day to prepare for the mobilisation process. What does that tell us, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe what it tells us, looking in the broader context of the events occurring around Zepa, is that once the forces of the Zvornik Brigade were pulled out of the Zepa operation and as that operation continued, or on the 15th kind of slowed down for lack of forces, that as the day or the next series of days wore on, it became apparent that the VRS did not have the required combat power to achieve the military solution that they wanted in Zepa, particularly with respect to General Mladic apparently pushing the issue harder to get a successful resolution before outside intervention that he perceived. So you have a series of incidents where forces have been pulled out of a main operation in Zepa. The operation is slowing down. You have the commander going through the resources and then making a decision at a point in time, and again we don't know when that decision was, that one of the sources of additional resources that he could pull was from the Bratunac Brigade, and that is the order that he did. So I believe that is the context in which to look at these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But just as an aside, why would General Krstic get involved in the situation? Why have none other than General Mladic? I mean, this is Drina Corps territory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I guess the best I can say on this one is that reading it in context with the proposal by Colonel Milanovic, if on the 15th of July the Drina Corps had no officers to -- who were capable of controlling this operation and that's why they chose Colonel Blagojevic to assume command of that, then when Colonel Blagojevic was then directed to go with his troops to Zepa, they still didn't have any other officers. And whether or not General Krstic became involved with the Main Staff and requested relief or requested assistance from other officers is an answer I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words what you're saying to us is: General Krstic could not, assuming Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic was available, General Krstic could not order him or place these assets under Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic's command, rather he would have to go to the Main Staff and then that order could come directly from the Main Staff down?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That would be the correct sequence of things that should have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just one last point. When these men are under Keserovic, I take it that is in keeping with the principle of unity in command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the men assigned the mission of sweeping the terrain?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I believe that's all I have for this segment. And why don't we move now to -- we're going to take a step back and we're going to go to the 11th of July. Now we're in Bratunac. Srebrenica has, in essence, fallen, and we're at the first meeting, okay? The first meeting between General Mladic and DutchBat, Lieutenant Colonel Karremans. Okay. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point in time we have the Main Staff, the head of the Main Staff on the ground. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we already know that this is -- that Bratunac falls within the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Because we do know, if we look at the rules, that a corps does in fact have a geographical designation of a zone of responsibility. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In fact, it's written in the rules, lest there be any misunderstanding. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the 1990 corps provisional rules, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade happened to be in the -- they happened to be located in or slightly outside the centre of Bratunac, Bratunac town, that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is -- it's not in the centre of town, no, sir. I'm not sure how far on the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's in the town but not in the centre.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that point in time, who is in control? Is it General Mladic, or at that point it would be General Zivanovic, because he's still, as far as we all agree on, the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In control of what, the meeting? The military events?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me rephrase. Who is in command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic is always in command. He's the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So wherever he goes, he's in command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and even where he doesn't go, he's still in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that also mean that when he's in command, he's also in control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he's exercising command, he is controlling, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And was he exercising command in Bratunac on the 11th, the afternoon of the 11th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The early evening hours of the meeting, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, even before --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Srebrenica the afternoon of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in command and control in Srebrenica when he's making that victory march and he's ordering the platoon commander, you know, the soldiers, go there, go there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is actually a very accurate description of what he's doing. He's in command, he's acting like a platoon commander, and he's doing just that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he's not only in command, but he's also in control. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when he orders someone to go, go to Potocari, go to Bratunac, he's giving an order, is he not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in some respects what he's doing is bombastic in that regard. My understanding is that he did at that time, although maybe not in that format, direct that the brigades and the forces from Srebrenica push forward to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, if my memory serves me correct, there is one snippet where we see Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, tall, strikingly good-looking man, fairly confident. Do I have my dates correct where in fact he seems to be raising a concern about the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Colonel Pandurevic was in Srebrenica at that time. And it is my understanding that he did raise a concern about the location of the 28th Infantry Division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a -- Srebrenica was the place that they dreamt of taking over, and now it had been a realisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Certainly the people from the Bratunac Brigade, many of whom resided there, were anxious to have their hometown liberated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But also they knew there was a 28 Division, and lo and behold, when they entered Srebrenica on the 11th, there was nobody there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The division had broken contact the prior evening and had moved out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm not a military man, but it would seem that there are three choices. One, they could have gone towards Zepa, not very logical or realistic, because they could -- there was passage still. Two, they could have gone to the Bandera triangle where they normally kept to themselves. Or they could have headed towards Tuzla, another path which they had taken over the years. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Those were the three general military options.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would seem to me from listening to your testimony that initially they thought that perhaps they had concealed themselves in the Bandera triangle, hence why they -- some forces were sent in that direction, I believe, on the 11th or 12th. And it was only after they had more or less left the Bratunac Brigade area and they were just about coming into contact with the Zvornik Brigade that they realised, here was a column, a fairly large column, a large column that was armed and moving towards Zepa. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sequence of events is not correct. As we have from the military documents and from some of the other conversations, reflect that the VRS believe that the 28th Infantry Division wasn't in the Bandera triangle and in fact, they had decided they were going to deploy it and try and make it out towards Tuzla. The first indications that they were getting that there was a significant military column forming and trying to make the breakthrough through the mine fields, again started based on the intercept evidence during the morning of -- or the early morning hours of 12 July, 1995 and by the afternoon hours of 12 July, and certainly by the early evening hours of 12 July, there was an awareness that the bulk of the column was trying to make it towards Tuzla, however the actual size and the military capacity of that column was still being downplayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Needless to say, when Pandurevic is there -- well, let me ask you this: Do you think his concerns, Pandurevic's concerns, at that time and place were legitimate, the ones that he's expressing to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In military -- pretty much in general military tactics, one of the things you do not want to do is lose contact with an opposing military force. You want to be in contact with it so you know where it is and what it's doing. And if I'm correct, Colonel Pandurevic's concern was that there was no contact with the 28th Division and they had no reliable intelligence information or combat information as to where it might be located and what it may be doing next. So it's a very significant and proper concern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yet, General Mladic exercising his command and control decided that he was going to do other things. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. As I understand it, from both the testimony of General Krstic and interviews with select brigade commanders, General Mladic was persuaded not to advance immediately on Potocari. And the units remained in and around the Srebrenica area consolidating and preparing for the next day's operations. So I think in that case his subordinates were able to convince him that that was not a prudent thing to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He cooled his jets and remained in place for a little bit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if General Mladic ever cooled his jets, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, when he was in Bratunac on the second meeting that took place between Mladic and the DutchBat and the representatives from the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that would be the roughly 1000 hour meeting -- I'm sorry 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the 11th. Who was in command and control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly General Mladic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where might his forward command post have been at that given moment? Was it the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, was it Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terms, his forward command post should have been the Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And where do you think they were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, say again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you think they were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do I think who was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His forward command post, do you think that's where it was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The Drina Corps forward command post was at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, or one of them was, and that would have been where the Main Staff would have deployed their forward command people, and by extension a command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason you stated earlier is that, one, that's where you have the communications centre. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Security reasons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be a valid one, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course for logistics as well. Every time you need something, if you're in the Hotel Fontana and that's your forward command post, it becomes virtually impossible, would it not, for him to function?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be difficult, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why they normally set it up so that it falls in the lower command post, because they realise that all of these logistics already existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I take it he doesn't have to ask permission from the commander of the Bratunac Brigade whether he can use the command post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does not have to ask permission. I suspect that that is assumed that when he comes here he will do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can make that assumption also when the commander of the Drina Corps comes and decides, as you have indicated, to put its command post, its forward command post at the command post of the Bratunac Brigade, again the Drina Corps commander doesn't need to ask permission of the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- now, when you have all three in that building, in that command post, Main Staff, that's their forward command post; Drina Corps, that's their forward command post; and the Bratunac Brigade, that's their command post; who is really exercising command and control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what echelon formation forces that we're talking about. The argument can be made that wherever General Mladic is, he exercises command and control. And as the commander of an army, that is, in a broad sense, exactly what happens. However, within the more stratified environment or military environment, commanders are going to exercise command and control generally within their competencies of command. So while certainly there are going there are going to be instances where General Mladic will give orders to officers that may be one or two echelons below him. That fact that General Mladic is in command and in control in Bratunac doesn't meant that suddenly General Zivanovic isn't. And when General Zivanovic is in command and control in Bratunac, it doesn't mean that Colonel Blagojevic isn't. It's no absolute in this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It all depends on what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just have an appointment at 12.00 at my son's school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no problems with that, Your Honour. Far be it for me to -- I can pick up tomorrow where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, very good. We'll resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
